name: Avesta
info: The Avesta is the corpus of religious texts of Zoroastrianism, composed orally in the Avestan language over several centuries, written down in the Sasanian era, and now surviving only in part in ritual and devotional manuscripts.

facts.made: Zoroastrian tradition holds that Ahura Mazda created the twenty-one nasks and that Zoroaster brought them to his patron Vishtaspa; scholars describe oral compositions by generations of poet-priests during the Avestan period
facts.form: Texts in the Avestan language, written in the Avestan alphabet; the Old Avestan layer (the Gathas) and the larger Young Avestan layer, grouped in the Yasna (72 sections), Visperad (24 sections), Vendidad (22 fragards), Khordeh Avesta and fragment collections
facts.where: More than 300 manuscripts are catalogued, kept in Iranian and Indian Zoroastrian traditions; the oldest surviving fragment (K1) dates to 1323 CE, and the Avestan Digital Archive has digitised 150 manuscripts
facts.known: the oldest texts in any Iranian language; the Gathas; the Yasna, Visperad and Vendidad liturgies; the Yashts, hymns to divinities; the Khordeh Avesta, or Little Avesta, for lay people; the loss of the Sasanian edition; Anquetil-Duperron's translations of 1771

t: The Avesta is the religious literature of Zoroastrianism, composed in Avestan, and it holds the oldest texts in any Iranian language.
Its texts were handed down orally for many centuries, and were written down only from around the 5th or 6th century CE, in the Sasanian era.
Only part of the Sasanian edition survives, in ritual and devotional manuscripts, the oldest fragment dating to 1323 CE.
dyk: Summaries in Zoroastrian texts of the 9th and 10th centuries indicate that only about one quarter of the Avestan sentences or verses they refer to can be found in the surviving texts.
ev: Many scholars consider a date close to this likely for the Old Avestan texts, within a possible range of 1500 to 900 BCE
The Young Avestan texts are thought to have been composed in the eastern part of Greater Iran, over a long period
The Sasanian era begins, the period in which the Avestan alphabet is created and the Avesta first written down
The Avestan corpus is written down for the first time, producing the comprehensive Sasanian Avesta
The oldest surviving fragment of an Avestan manuscript, known as K1, is dated to this year
Abraham Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron travels to India and finds the texts among the Parsi communities
Westergaard publishes the first critical edition of the Avesta
Geldner produces the edition that remains the standard one for the surviving corpus

sections.origins:
The Avesta is the corpus of religious texts of Zoroastrianism. All its texts are composed in the Avestan language and written in the Avestan alphabet. The individual texts were originally oral compositions, made over several centuries during what scholars call the Avestan period, which may range from the 15th century BCE to the 4th century BCE.

Scholars divide the texts into two layers, Old Avestan and Young Avestan, which belong to different chronological strata. For the Old Avestan material a time frame between 1500 and 900 BCE is considered possible, and many regard a date close to 1000 BCE as likely. The Old Avestan texts contain no geographical references, so where they were composed cannot be said. The Young Avestan texts, which form most of the extant Avesta, come from a later stage, perhaps 900 to 400 BCE, and their geographical references have led to a consensus that they were composed in the eastern part of Greater Iran.

The Avesta represents the largest literature of the Old Iranian period and contains the oldest texts in any Iranian language. The word Avesta itself comes from Zoroastrian works of the 9th and 10th centuries, where it appears as Middle Persian abestāg, and its literal meaning is uncertain.
sections.content:
The extant Avesta is organised by the ceremonies in which its texts are used. The Yasna, from a word meaning worship or oblations, is recited in the main Zoroastrian liturgy and has 72 sections called ha. Its central part, Yasna 14 to 58, is the Staota Yesnya, which formed one of the volumes of the Sasanian Avesta. The Visperad, 24 sections called karde, is interleaved with the Yasna in its own liturgy. The Vendidad, a name that derives from words meaning given against the demons, has 22 sections called fragards, framed as discussions between Ahura Mazda and Zoroaster, and it deals with laws rather than recording a ceremony.

The Khordeh Avesta, or Little Avesta, is a collection of devotional texts aimed at lay people, whereas the Yasna, Visperad and Vendidad are performed only by priests, typically inside a fire temple. Most of its manuscripts contain the five Nyayesh prayers, the five Gah invocations, at least some of the 21 Yashts, the 30 Sih-rozag and the four Afrinagan prayers. The Yashts are hymns, each dedicated to a particular divinity or divine concept.

More than 20 collections of minor or incomplete texts are known as fragments.
sections.making:
According to the Denkard, a Zoroastrian text of the Pahlavi books, the twenty-one nasks, or books, of the Avesta were created by Ahura Mazda and brought by Zoroaster to his patron Vishtaspa. The same tradition tells that the Avesta was destroyed or dispersed after Alexander's conquest, was gathered again under a Parthian ruler named Valaksh, and was then collated by the early Sasanian priest Tansar and completed by Adurbad Mahraspandan, with a final revision in the 6th century CE under Khosrow I. The oldest surviving versions of these tales date from the ninth to 11th centuries, and modern scholarship generally rejects the account of the period before the Sasanian era.

Scholars instead hold that the texts were handed down orally and independently of one another for most of their history. The Old Avestan texts crystallised early, and the Gathic texts seem to have been transmitted with the highest accuracy. The Young Avestan texts stayed fluid for some time, composed partly afresh by each generation of poet-priests, until a second crystallisation, which Skjærvø and Kreyenbroek correlate with the adoption of Zoroastrianism by the Achaemenids. Persian- and Median-speaking priests then became the main transmitters, and may have preserved the texts as faithfully as possible without an active command of Avestan.
sections.reception:
The Sasanian Avesta was, according to the Denkard, organised into 21 nasks, to mirror the 21-word Ahuna Vairya manthra, each of whose three lines has seven words. The nasks fell into three groups of seven: a Gathic group containing the Gathas and long commentaries on them, a manthric group, and a legal group.

The Sasanian edition is generally assumed to have contained a full translation and commentary in Middle Persian, called Zand, since references to it quote the Middle Persian translation and the texts derived directly from it, the Vendidad, the Herbedestan and the Nerangestan, all include a Zand. These translations are generally considered the oldest and most faithful.

In Europe, the study of Zoroastrianism dates to the 18th century. Anquetil-Duperron travelled to India in 1755, found the texts among the Parsi communities and published French translations in 1771. They were at first dismissed as a forgery in poor Sanskrit, but were ultimately vindicated. Later translations include the English volumes by Darmesteter and Mills in the Sacred Books of the East series, between 1880 and 1887, and Darmesteter's French version of 1892 and 1893, which rested mostly on the Middle Persian translation. Fritz Wolff's German translation of 1910 translated the Avestan directly and is generally seen as superior.
sections.survival:
It was not until around the 5th or 6th century CE that the Avestan corpus was written down in the newly developed Avestan alphabet, giving the Sasanian Avesta, which is seen as a turning point because it separates purely oral from written transmission. That edition was lost at some point after the fall of the Sasanian empire. The oldest surviving manuscript of an Avestan text, K1, is dated to 1323 CE, and most extant manuscripts date from after the 17th century. More than 300 are catalogued. The history between the Sasanian edition and these manuscripts is unknown.

Summaries in texts of the 9th and 10th centuries show that the Sasanian Avesta was much larger, and only about a quarter of the sentences or verses they refer to survive, so an indeterminable number of juridical, historical and legendary texts have been lost. The most valuable portions, including all the oldest texts, appear to have survived. The likely reason is that they were in regular liturgical use and known by heart by the priests, so they did not depend on particular manuscripts.

The Vendidad's Juddēwdād nask is the only nask of the Sasanian Avesta to survive intact. No new authoritative edition has been produced by the Zoroastrian community since the Sasanian one was lost.
sections.legacy:
Scholarly editions followed the arrival of the manuscripts in the West. Westergaard published the first critical edition in 1852, based mostly on manuscripts collected by Rask. Between 1886 and 1896 Geldner edited the Yasna, the Visperad, the Khordeh Avesta and the Vendidad from significantly more manuscripts, and his work has remained the standard edition of the surviving corpus. It is a scholarly edition and is not canonical in a religious sense.

In the early 20th century the Zoroastrian legend of a Parthian collation led to a search for a Parthian archetype of the Avesta. Friedrich Carl Andreas proposed in 1902 that odd spellings reflected errors made in transcription from Pahlavi scripts. The search was increasingly criticised in the 1940s and was abandoned in the 1950s after Karl Hoffmann showed that the inconsistencies came from unconscious changes in oral transmission.

New manuscripts, especially from Iran, have cast doubt on the view that all derive from one Sasanian archetype, and the surviving texts are now seen as witnesses of a living liturgical tradition. This led to the Avestan Digital Archive, which as of 2013 had digitised 150 manuscripts and put 80 of them online, and to the Corpus Avesticum Berolinense, which edits manuscripts within their ritual context.

summary: The Avesta is the body of Zoroastrian religious texts in the Avestan language. Composed orally over centuries and first written down in the Sasanian era, it survives only in part, in ritual and devotional manuscripts, the oldest fragment dated 1323 CE.
references: Karl Hoffmann, Der Sasanidische Archetypus – Untersuchungen zu Schreibung und Lautgestalt des Avestischen (Reichert Verlag, 1989)
Helmut Humbach, The Gathas of Zarathushtra and the Other Old Avestan Texts (Winter, 1991)
Michiel de Vaan, Introduction to Avestan (Brill, 2014)

notes: start -1000 is the article's likely date for Old Avestan (range 1500-900 BCE); the Avestan period as a whole may run from the 15th to the 4th century BCE.
The article gives the written transmission as 'around the 5th or 6th century CE' while the lead places it in the Sasanian era (224 to 651 CE); both are given.
The article names Valaksh as 'one of the Vologases' and dates Tansar under Ardashir I and Shapur I; only some of this is used.
The Visperad liturgy is described as an extension of the Yasna liturgy via the Vendidad; the article's wording is slightly loose.
The Pahlavi books' tales are called legends and myths in the article; the draft attributes them to the Denkard without that label.
